He finds himself thinking about the woman sometimes, wondering whether she still carries it too, whether she knows that a man three registers away has not stopped seeing her fall.

He came to therapy at Aroha's quiet insistence. He sat in the first session with his hands on his knees and said, carefully, that he wasn't sure he deserved to be there.

Raúl Mendez was a 70-year-old widowed dentist who had spent most of his life in a busy Latin American immigrant neighborhood, treating generations of families in the same small office near a downtown bus line. The terrorist attack that changed him happened years earlier while he was crossing a public square after work, still in his white coat, when a vehicle and armed men turned a crowded evening into chaos. He remembered the sudden crack of gunshots, the shouting, the uniforms moving through the smoke, and the terrible confusion of not knowing who was protecting whom. Even now, when the memory returned, it did not come to him as a clear story; it hit him in fragments so vivid that he would have to stop speaking, his chest tightening as if he were back among the noise, the panic, and the sight of bodies diving for cover. He said he could not seem to put the frightening event into words, and that was part of why it kept coming back with such force. When it did, the whole scene overwhelmed him emotionally, as if the terror were happening again through all his senses at once.

Over time, certain things around him became dangerous in a way that seemed obvious to him. A man in a police uniform entering his building, a television discussion about military action, or the sharp pop of a car backfiring outside the clinic could drop him into the same state of alarm. Those moments often carried him straight back to the attack, and he would feel the memory surge up before he could steady himself. He became intensely watchful when he was out in the waiting room or walking to his car, scanning the faces of other people for signs that they might mean harm, and checking exits as soon as he entered a room or building. In the office, where he had once moved with practiced ease, he now positioned himself near the door and noticed every sudden sound in the hallway. He described feeling on high alert whenever he heard something unexpected or loud, as though another blast could happen without warning. The triggers and the memory fed one another: a uniform, a loud noise, or even a conversation about soldiers would revive the sensory force of the event, and once the memory took hold, it made those same cues feel even more charged the next time they appeared.

Raúl tried to protect himself by managing the fear in ways that seemed sensible at first. He began avoiding news reports about attacks or conflicts that reminded him of what had happened, and he carried a weapon more often than before, telling himself that if he stayed prepared he might not be helpless again. Yet these habits came with a cost. The more he replayed the event in his mind, the more he blamed himself for not having done enough that day, and that self-accusation kept the scene active rather than settled. At night he would go over the square, the gunfire, and the uniforms again and again, searching for the moment he believed he should have acted differently. Those periods of rumination often ended with the same wave of sensory recollection, and once the memory returned so vividly, he was left too overwhelmed to think in a calmer way. Afterward he would notice that he was more likely to avoid the news again, more likely to keep the weapon close, and more certain that danger was always near. His efforts to control the fear also seemed to teach him to look harder for it: carrying the weapon and replaying the event made him watch people more closely, scan every doorway, and stay braced for loud sounds, which in turn kept the attack feeling present.

In the clinic and in the neighborhood, this pattern had narrowed his life. He no longer stayed for coffee after work and rarely attended community gatherings where military topics might come up or where uniformed officers were present. He had become more isolated since his wife died, and his adult daughter worried that he seemed to be living as if the attack were still waiting outside the office door. What finally brought him to seek help was the growing burden of constantly being on guard, especially after he startled badly at a sudden bang in the dental lab and spent the rest of the day watching every person who walked past the front window. Raúl said he was tired of carrying fear everywhere and tired of the way it kept pulling him back into the same images and the same blame. What he feared most was that he would never feel safe enough to let his guard down, but what he hoped for was simpler: to walk into a room, hear an unexpected sound, and not have his whole body tell him that the terror was starting again.

He was twenty-six when the hurricane came-three years ago now, though it might as well be yesterday. The storm wasn't supposed to hit their town directly, but it shifted course overnight. By the time the warnings came, it was too late to leave. He remembers the sound most of all: a deep, unending roar, like a freight train running through the living room. Then the walls began to groan, and the roof lifted in sections, letting in the sky and the rain and the wind all at once. He and his mother huddled in the hallway closet, the only place left that felt solid. She held his hand so tightly he thought the bones would break. When the ceiling collapsed in the next room, the shock wave threw them against the far wall. He felt something crack in his shoulder, but he couldn't tell if it was his or hers.

They survived. His mother spent three weeks in the hospital with a punctured lung and a broken pelvis. He healed quickly-just a separated shoulder, some cuts. But the inside of him never healed the same way. Even now, when the wind picks up outside his apartment, he finds himself holding his breath, scanning the room for a place to hide. His sleep is broken by fragments of that night: the roar, the darkness, the smell of wet plaster. He wakes with his heart slamming against his ribs, convinced the ceiling is about to come down again.

He works as a salesperson at a car dealership, a job that used to come naturally. He was the guy who could chat up anyone, crack jokes, build rapport. Now, the open showroom floor feels exposed. The large windows make him edgy. When a customer mentions an upcoming storm on the news, his stomach tightens, and he has to excuse himself to the restroom to reset. His monthly numbers have slipped, not because he doesn't know the product, but because he struggles to sustain the easygoing energy customers expect. Twice this month, a manager pulled him aside to ask if everything was okay. He said yes, because there is no way to explain that the sound of a slamming car door makes him flinch and see the closet door buckling.

He avoids driving on rainy days. If he sees flood warnings on his phone, he takes a different route to work, even if it adds forty minutes. He canceled a date last week because the forecast showed a chance of thunderstorms. The woman was understanding, but he felt a familiar shame-the kind that tells him he is becoming someone smaller than he used to be. At night, he checks the weather app obsessively before turning off the light, sometimes three or four times. He keeps a flashlight and a bottle of water under the bed, just in case. He knows it's irrational. The house he grew up in was rebuilt. The odds of another hurricane hitting directly are low. But knowing doesn't stop the tightness from creeping into his chest when the barometer drops.

His social life has narrowed. He used to go out with friends from work, but now he makes excuses. Crowds feel unpredictable; loud noises make him jumpy. On the rare night he stays out late, he drinks too much to quiet the hypervigilance, and the next day he calls in sick with a headache. He has not spoken to his mother about it. She recovered, but she doesn't like to talk about the storm. They talk about everything else-weather, her garden, his job-never that night. He thinks maybe she has moved on. He wonders why he cannot.

A few weeks ago, he was driving home when he passed a construction site where a crew was tearing down a damaged building. The sound of the wrecking ball hitting concrete made his hands lock on the wheel. He had to pull over, heart racing, palms sweating, a wave of nausea rising. He sat there for fifteen minutes, telling himself it was just a job site, just a machine. But the feeling did not fully leave until he was inside his apartment with the door locked and the blinds drawn.

He has not told anyone the full story. Not his friends, not his coworkers, not the doctor he saw for his shoulder. He carries it alone, like a weight he cannot put down. Some days he wonders if the storm will ever really end for him, or if he will always be that person in the closet, waiting for the ceiling to fall.

Samir, a 26-year-old Middle Eastern non-binary veterinarian, came to treatment after months of trying to keep their life looking ordinary while feeling increasingly unable to relax anywhere outside a few familiar spaces. The robbery happened on a winter evening after a late shift, when Samir was walking to their car with their work bag slung over one shoulder and still half-focused on a sick dog they had been treating. The parking lot was dim, the air sharp and metallic, and as they neared their car a man came up fast enough that Samir had only a second to register the sudden movement before he was close, demanding their wallet and phone. Samir remembered the hard, immediate jolt of fear, the way their body seemed to decide before their mind did. They handed over what he wanted, careful and quiet, trying to keep the situation calm. In the days afterward, Samir found themselves telling people, and sometimes themselves, that it had not really happened or that it had not been that bad, as if saying it enough times might make the memory feel smaller. Yet the event remained oddly vivid and fragmented at once. When they tried to explain it, they would lose the thread midway through, stopping and restarting, unable to hold the sequence together in a way that felt coherent. At unexpected moments, the memory would return with full force from something ordinary in the surroundings: the sound of footsteps behind them on a sidewalk, the sight of a shadow moving quickly beside a parked car, the smell of cold pavement and cigarette smoke drifting past outside a store. Even a trace of that smell could bring back the whole scene before Samir had time to prepare for it.

Over the following weeks, Samir began moving through the world as though danger might appear at any moment. They constantly scanned their surroundings for signs of threat, their eyes moving automatically from faces to hands to exits, then over their shoulder to check whether someone was following them. They did this in hospital corridors, in the clinic parking lot, and on the short walk from their apartment to the corner store. Outside, they became increasingly reluctant to go out unless they had to, and what had once been an ordinary errand now required planning, reassurance, and resolve. At home, too, the sense of being watchful did not ease; even inside their own apartment, Samir remained on guard, listening for sounds in the hallway and reacting to every unexpected noise from the street below. They had come to believe that they had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next, and that other people could not really be relied upon to notice, prevent, or soften danger in time. This belief was not expressed as drama so much as as a quiet, hardened practicality, the kind that made them double-check locks, choose seats with clear views of the door, and sit tense rather than comfortable even when their partner was beside them.

Samir's work as a veterinarian had also become a setting where the aftermath of the robbery kept intruding into the present. When they left the clinic after evening appointments, the parking lot could suddenly feel menacing in a way it had not before, and they would delay leaving, text their partner, or wait for another staff member to walk out with them. The drive home became a careful scan of mirrors and intersections, and the walk from the car to the building was now done briskly, with repeated glances behind them. The changes were hard to hide from the person they were in a relationship with, who noticed Samir's vigilance and the way they seemed to tense whenever someone approached too quickly from behind. Samir still tried to preserve a version of themselves that had once been happy, but privately they felt that the person they had been was gone, replaced by someone who was always bracing for the next bad thing. They described themselves as miserable now, a word that seemed to carry both grief and exhaustion, as if ordinary ease had become inaccessible.

Despite the strain, Samir continued to function at work and in the relationship, often by becoming overly compliant when they felt threatened or cornered, agreeing quickly, smoothing over discomfort, and trying not to draw attention. It was a way of keeping situations from escalating, a style of submission that made sense to them in the moment and that they recognized as something they slipped into almost automatically. Still, the cost accumulated. The robbery kept returning in sensory flashes, the vigilance never fully settled, and their world kept shrinking around routes, places, and times of day that felt safer. What finally brought Samir to seek help was the growing realization that they could no longer keep pretending the event had not changed them. They were frightened by how often they were on edge, by how hard it had become to go out, and by the possibility that this narrowed, guarded way of living might become permanent. More than anything, Samir wanted to feel safe enough to move through the world without checking behind them every few seconds, and to believe again that not every stranger or street corner was a threat waiting to happen.

Mrs. Chen arranges the pyramids of oranges with a practiced, steady hand, the motion so ingrained it requires no thought. For forty years, this small grocery store has been her world-the sweet dust of rice in the air, the chime of the bell above the door, the familiar faces of her neighbors. It used to be a place of comfort, of predictable rhythm. Now, the chime of the bell makes her flinch.

It wasn't always this way. She remembers a time when her energy felt boundless, when she and her husband, Wei Sr., worked from dawn until dusk, building this life for their son. Wei was a bright, energetic boy, his laughter the real music of the shop. Then, when he was nine, the music stopped. It started with bruises that wouldn't fade and a weariness that sleep couldn't fix. The diagnosis-acute lymphoblastic leukemia-was a foreign, terrifying word that cleaved her life into a before and an after.

The two years that followed are a smear of memories she tries constantly to push away, but they bleed through at the edges of her days. The chemical tang of antiseptic is what comes back most often, a smell she now catches in the bleach she uses to mop the store floor, sending a cold spike of dread through her chest. She remembers the relentless, cheerful beep of the IV pump, a sound she sometimes imagines she can still hear in the dead of night, jerking her from a shallow sleep. She spent countless nights in a vinyl chair that cracked when she shifted, watching Wei's small chest rise and fall, her entire being focused on that single, fragile motion. She felt like a soldier on watch, convinced that if she ever relaxed, if she ever looked away, he would slip away from her.

Wei got better. He survived, endured the brutal treatments, and grew into a healthy, successful man with a family of his own. Everyone told her it was a miracle, a reason to celebrate. And she does celebrate, on the surface. She hosts family dinners, dotes on her grandchildren, and smiles when her husband says how lucky they are. But the soldier inside her never stood down. The war ended, but she is still crouched in the trench.

Her husband doesn't understand why she still calls Wei every single night, her breath held until she hears his voice. He doesn't see the panic that flashes in her eyes when her granddaughter coughs for more than a day. He tells her to let it go, to be grateful for the present. She feels a profound sense of shame for her inability to do so, a guilt that isolates her. It feels like a betrayal to her son's health to still live in the shadow of his sickness.

In the shop, a mother comes in with a pale, listless child, and Mrs. Chen has to turn away, her heart hammering against her ribs as she pretends to be busy restocking a shelf. She finds her temper is shorter now, her patience with customers worn thin. The joy she once took in her work has been replaced by a low, humming vigilance. She feels disconnected from the simple pleasures of her life, a ghost going through the motions.

At night, after locking the shop door and turning off the lights, she stands for a moment in the quiet dark. The fear is always there, a cold weight in her stomach. The crisis is twenty years in the past, her son is a grown man, and her life is, by all accounts, good. Yet, she cannot shake the feeling that she is still in that hospital room, perpetually waiting for the next alarm to sound, for the other shoe to inevitably, devastatingly, drop.

Mark had been a firefighter for a decade before he took the two-month leave to volunteer with a relief agency. He was used to controlled chaos, to running towards danger that had a name and a shape. The war zone was different. The danger there was formless, an atmospheric pressure. The traumatic event itself wasn't a dramatic firefight but a moment of sudden, incomprehensible violence. He was organizing medical supplies in the concrete basement of a field clinic when a car bomb detonated in the street outside. The world became a concussion of sound and force. The lights went out, the air filled with thick, choking dust, and the ceiling sagged, raining down debris. The only way out was a narrow, partially collapsed stairwell, and the panicked rush of strangers in the pitch-dark felt as dangerous as the failing structure itself.

When he returned home to Chicago, his wife, Chloe, noticed he was different. He was quieter, and the easy-going physicality he once had was gone, replaced by a tense stillness. At first, the changes were subtle. In restaurants, he would insist on a table near the door. At the movies, he would only take an aisle seat at the back. He told himself it was just being tactical, an extension of his professional training, but the behaviour soon hardened into a rigid rule. The simple act of entering a room became an exercise in threat assessment; before he could sit down, he had to locate every possible exit, his mind mapping escape routes he would never use. This constant rehearsal of disaster prevention sent a powerful, unending message to his nervous system: you are never safe. The world, his brain concluded, was a place that required a perpetual exit strategy.

This deep-seated conviction that threat was imminent began to poison every aspect of his life. At home, the place he once recharged, he felt perpetually on guard, startling at the sound of a delivery truck in the street or the rattle of the pipes. He would walk the house at night, checking locks he knew were secure. The feeling of safety had been hollowed out, replaced with a low hum of anxiety. His strategies, meant to keep him safe, were instead the very things convincing him he was in constant danger. He started avoiding the fire station's gym, telling his crew he was nursing a bad knee. The truth was that the sensation of a pounding heart and ragged breath-the very feelings of exertion and life-had become indistinguishable from the memory of clawing his way up that collapsed stairwell, gasping for air. By avoiding exercise, he denied his body any chance to relearn that a racing pulse could be benign, cementing the idea that any internal arousal was a herald of doom.

The most insidious change was his relationship with happiness. One evening, Chloe shared some good news about her job, her face lit with a joy he hadn't seen in months. He felt a flicker of warmth in his own chest, a genuine moment of shared happiness, but it was immediately followed by a cold wave of panic. Letting his guard down felt like an invitation for another blind-sided attack. He pushed the positive emotion away, his expression going blank. He saw the light in Chloe's eyes dim, replaced by a familiar look of hurt confusion. This emotional suppression kept him locked in a state of hypervigilance, which he interpreted as necessary readiness. His attempts to control his world were shrinking it, and the person he loved most was now on the outside of the fortress he had built. He came to therapy after his captain gave him a formal warning about his performance in training drills, threatening to move him to a desk job. The thought of losing the one identity he had left, of no longer being a firefighter, was more terrifying than any threat he could imagine. He sat in the consulting room, a man trapped inside his own alarm system, quietly asking if it was possible to ever feel safe again.

Marisol had been working the late shift at a busy bar in downtown Phoenix when her younger brother, Daniel, was struck by a drunk driver on the way home from her place. She remembered the evening with an unsettling sharpness that still caught her off guard: the fluorescent light in the kitchen when she had asked him to "just wait five minutes," the sound of his keys hitting the counter, the flash of his red jacket as he stepped out the door. Other parts of the night were blank in a way that troubled her, as if the mind had cut holes in the film; she could not reconstruct the exact sequence after the phone call, only fragments of police uniforms, the cold air outside, and the feeling of her own hands shaking. What stayed with her most were images rather than a full story, and those images came back with painful clarity.

In the weeks that followed, Marisol had come to believe that the crash happened because of the way she acted. She replayed her insistence that Daniel leave, her irritation when he lingered, and she was certain that if she had just been more patient he would have stayed inside. That belief hardened into a broader suspicion that people were not what they seemed and that she could not rely on other people to keep anyone safe. The memory itself seemed to feed those conclusions: the vivid pictures of the night made the accident feel pinned to her own choices, while the blank stretches made her mind fill in the gaps with worst-case explanations, leaving her more convinced that she had missed something important and failed him.

Those appraisals began to shape how Marisol lived. She stopped watching the news after stumbling across reports about pedestrians hit by cars or families mourning sudden losses; even hearing a headline in the bar during the lunch rush made her turn away and wipe the counter harder, as if she could scrub the images out of her head. She also tried hard to control her emotions, keeping her face composed with customers and with her boyfriend, Luis, because she feared that once she started crying or talking about Daniel she would fall apart and never stop. The same belief that she had caused the tragedy made seeking medical or psychological help feel impossible to her. She worried that if she told the wrong person, they would judge her carelessness, ask questions she could not answer, or confirm what she already suspected about herself. So she put off appointments, ignored reminders from her primary care clinic, and decided she could manage on her own.

Yet the effort to hold everything in place only made the memories more intrusive. A siren outside the bar, a red jacket at the end of the counter, the metallic clink of keys in a customer's hand, or a news clip glimpsed on a screen she had meant not to watch could pull her straight back to that night. When the pictures came, they arrived with the same vivid, detailed force as before: Daniel's face in profile, the kitchen light, the door closing. The more often the images returned, the more Marisol concluded that she must not have been careful enough, must have overlooked something, must somehow still be responsible. That renewed self-blame made her tighten her efforts to avoid anything that might stir the memory or expose her to other people's opinions, and she began to work extra shifts and keep herself occupied rather than sit with Luis at home where silence gave her too much room to think.

Over months, the pattern narrowed her life. She became more guarded at work, less likely to check in with regulars about their families, and more impatient with herself whenever she felt emotion rising. The bar, once a place where she moved easily through noise and conversation, now required constant vigilance for reminders she did not want. She had started to live as though distance from bad news, from her own feelings, and from other people's help might protect her from another catastrophe, yet each new avoidance seemed to leave her with the same troubling pictures and the same conviction that she had failed Daniel. By the time she finally came for help, it was after Luis told her he no longer knew how to reach her and after she realized she was spending more and more of her nights bracing for the next image to hit. What she feared most was that she had already proven herself the kind of person who lets terrible things happen; what she hoped for, though she said it quietly, was to find a way to remember Daniel without feeling that she had to keep disappearing from everyone else's life.

Frank, a 47-year-old bus driver, had spent two decades navigating the city's streets with a calm stoicism. That changed six months ago. During a routine traffic stop for a supposed broken taillight, he was pulled from his personal car, mistaken for a suspect in a nearby robbery. The encounter was brief but brutal, ending with him pinned to the pavement, the officer's knee on his back, before the mistake was realized. There was no apology, just a gruff "you're free to go." The physical bruises faded, but the incident left an imprint that reshaped his world.

Initially, it was just the jumpiness. A siren would wail in the distance, and Frank's hands would tighten on the large steering wheel of his bus. Soon, the sight of a police cruiser parked by the side of the road was enough to trigger a hot surge of anger that made it difficult to concentrate on the traffic ahead. This constant state of threat began to bleed into his perception of everything. Living at that pitch of alertness, his mind automatically scanned for and snagged on any potential sign of authority, turning his daily bus route into a landscape dense with reminders of his vulnerability. After months of simmering irritability and hypervigilance, Frank came to the conclusion that this must be what the world was really like: a hostile place where danger was always lurking. This raw, ever-present sense of threat solidified his belief that people, in general, simply can't be trusted. This new conviction that the world was hostile primed him to see threats everywhere, meaning the previously routine sight of a police car was no longer just part of the city's backdrop, but a specific and immediate warning.

This new conviction governed his life. Convinced that the world was a dangerous place, he began checking the doors and locks at his apartment three, four, sometimes five times before he could even think about sleeping. His belief that people were untrustworthy transformed his bus from a moving community into an isolated capsule. He stopped making small talk with the regulars on his route and started taking his breaks alone in the depot, avoiding the easy camaraderie of the staff room. The more he isolated himself, the more he felt the truth of his own conclusion: he had lost his connection to his community, a ghost driving the city streets. This profound sense of disconnection only served to amplify his vigilance; his avoidance of others made him feel more exposed when he had to interact, ratcheting up his baseline sense of threat.

The cycle has now become self-sustaining and vicious. A sudden, intrusive memory of the officer's face flashing in his mind will cause him to instinctively raise a hand to his cheek, as if to shield himself from a blow that isn't coming. This action, a fleeting attempt to hide his face, deepens his shame and sense of alienation. The constant, exhausting feeling of being on high alert drives him to blast the television the moment he gets home, a wall of sensory distraction to keep the silence-and the thoughts-at bay. In the rare moments of quiet, perhaps after turning down the TV to check the locks again, the intrusive memories seem to rush in to fill the void. His conviction that people are untrustworthy also seems to prime him, making even a brief mention of law enforcement on the radio feel like a direct, personal threat.

Last week, his supervisor called him in. There had been complaints: an angry outburst at a passenger who asked for directions, and a report of him driving erratically after passing a police checkpoint. He was given a formal warning and a recommendation to seek support. Frank sat in the office, unable to explain that the world felt like a minefield, that his concentration shattered every time he saw a uniform, that he felt utterly alone in his fear. He came to therapy not with hope, but with the quiet desperation of a man afraid of losing the last piece of structure in his life: his job. He doesn't know if he can ever feel safe again, but he is terrified of what will happen if he doesn't try.

Vignette: Emmanuel

Emmanuel is a 62-year-old married man who has spent the better part of four decades doing work that most people cannot bring themselves to imagine. As a bomb disposal technician, he has always understood that danger is simply part of the contract - something to be managed through training, discipline, and the kind of quiet courage that never announces itself. He has defused devices in the field, worked in conditions that would paralyze an ordinary person, and come home each time to his wife, Amara, and their grown children. For most of his career, he believed that his composure was something close to permanent.

That belief ended three years ago.

During a routine sweep of a suspected weapons storage facility, Emmanuel and two colleagues encountered what appeared to be a compromised canister of industrial chemical agent. Before proper containment protocols could be executed, there was a partial release. Emmanuel was closest to the source. He remembers the smell first - something sweet and wrong at the same time - and then a burning sensation across his face and throat that arrived before he had time to reach for his mask. He was evacuated, decontaminated, and hospitalized for eleven days. His colleagues were treated and discharged within a week. Emmanuel's respiratory damage was more significant, and the uncertainty about long-term effects was never fully resolved by the medical team.

He returned to modified administrative duties within three months, insisting to his supervisors and to Amara that he was fine. He was not fine.

The smell is the thing that undoes him most reliably. Cleaning products, certain perfumes, even the particular sharpness of cold morning air can send him back to that room with a speed and completeness that leaves him gripping whatever surface is nearest. During these moments, Emmanuel does not feel as though he is remembering - he feels as though he is still there, still breathing something that is trying to kill him. His heart pounds, his throat tightens, and for a few seconds that feel much longer, he is certain he is dying. He has stopped using the communal kitchen at work because a colleague's solvent-based hand cleaner triggered an episode so severe that he had to leave the building and sit in his car for forty minutes before he could drive.

At home, Amara has learned not to light scented candles. She has not said anything about this directly, and neither has he, but they both know. Emmanuel finds himself checking the windows before bed - not for intruders, but to make sure nothing is getting in. He sleeps in fragments, waking between two and four in the morning with his chest tight and his mind already running through the sequence of events at the facility, searching, as it always does, for the moment where he could have done something differently. He has not found it. He keeps looking.

He is quieter than he used to be. His eldest son mentioned it at a family dinner, framing it gently as a question about whether his father was tired, and Emmanuel changed the subject with the practiced ease of a man who has spent a lifetime managing what others see. What his son does not know is that Emmanuel had excused himself to the bathroom twenty minutes earlier because the smell of the gas stove had made his hands shake.

He still goes to work. He still reads the technical briefings, still consults on cases, still presents himself as a man with thirty-eight years of experience who knows what he is doing. And in many respects, he does. But he also knows that he has not been inside an active disposal site since the incident, and that when his supervisor recently suggested he might return to light field work, Emmanuel agreed immediately and then spent the following night awake until dawn, watching the ceiling and telling himself that he would be ready.

He is not sure he believes it.

Marcus

Marcus has been cutting hair for thirty-four years. He knows the rhythms of his work the way a musician knows their instrument-the weight of scissors in his palm, the angle of the blade, the way different textures of hair respond to his touch. His small shop sits on a corner in the neighborhood where he's lived most of his adult life, and his clients are people he's known for decades. Some have been coming to him since they were boys themselves.

Three years ago, on a Tuesday evening in October, Marcus was closing up. He'd just finished sweeping, the smell of hair tonic and soap still hanging in the air, when two men pushed through the door. He remembers their faces clearly-something he wishes he didn't. One held a knife. The other went straight for the register while the man with the blade kept the knife pointed at Marcus's chest, telling him not to move, not to look at them, not to do anything stupid. Marcus complied. He'd heard stories, knew better than to resist. It was over in minutes. They took the day's cash-about three hundred dollars-and left him standing alone in his shop, shaking.

The police came. They took a report. They never found the men.

Now, three years later, Marcus still closes his shop at four o'clock instead of six. He tells his wife, Amara, it's because he's getting older, wants more time at home. The truth is different. As the sun begins to set, his chest tightens. He finds himself checking the locks repeatedly, positioning himself so he can see the door. His hands shake. He's stopped working on Tuesdays altogether, though he doesn't acknowledge why.

When clients come in, Marcus struggles to concentrate. His mind splits between the present-the familiar weight of scissors, the small talk about grandchildren and work-and the past. He finds himself studying new customers' hands, looking for weapons. Last month, a young man came in wearing a dark jacket, and Marcus's vision narrowed. His breathing became shallow. He made an excuse and stepped into the back room for ten minutes, gripping the edge of the sink until the panic subsided.

At night, Marcus lies awake beside Amara, his body rigid with tension. When he does sleep, he dreams of the knife, of his own helplessness. He wakes gasping, sometimes shouting. Amara has learned not to touch him when he first wakes; his startle response is severe. She lies quietly, waiting for him to recognize where he is.

He's become irritable with Amara over small things-a noise she makes while eating, a question about his day. Then guilt washes over him. She doesn't deserve this. He knows that. He apologizes, but the anger returns unpredictably, a storm he can't control.

Marcus has lost weight. He used to enjoy the meals Amara prepared, but now food tastes like nothing. He's withdrawn from his friends, declined invitations to the monthly poker game he'd played in for twenty years. The thought of being in a crowded room, unable to see all the exits, makes his stomach clench.

He hasn't told anyone about the nightmares, the hypervigilance, the way he sometimes feels like he's back in that shop, frozen and powerless. He tells himself he should be over it by now. He survived. No one was hurt. But the fear remains, coiled inside him, waiting.

Amir is a 27-year-old physical therapist who came to therapy reluctantly, at his wife's urging, after months of what he called "not being himself." He is a tall, broad-shouldered man with a carefully neutral expression, but his hands tremble slightly as he sits down, and he chooses the chair farthest from the door. He speaks in a low, deliberate voice, often pausing to swallow before continuing.

The event that changed everything happened two years ago, on a Friday evening after a long shift at the outpatient clinic where he worked at the time. A male colleague, someone Amir had trusted and considered a friend, asked him to stay late to "review a case." When they were alone in the treatment room, the colleague stepped close, and Amir caught the sharp, woody scent of a new cologne-something expensive, something unfamiliar. Before Amir could move away, the colleague's hand was on his shoulder, then sliding down his back. Amir froze. He did not scream. He did not push back. He stood there, his body rigid, as the colleague's hands moved lower, as the cologne filled his nostrils, as a dull, grinding pain spread through his lower back-an old injury flaring under the pressure of being bent over the treatment table. When it was over, the colleague straightened his lab coat, smiled, and said, "I think we understand each other now." Amir walked out of the clinic in silence, drove home in silence, and never told anyone what happened. He quit the job two weeks later, citing "personal reasons."

In the months that followed, Amir began to notice changes he could not explain. He found himself scanning every room he entered, cataloging exits, noting the positions of men who stood too close. The startle response was the first thing he could not hide. A hand on his shoulder at a grocery store made him flinch so violently that the other person stepped back, apologizing. His wife, reaching for his arm in bed, would find him already tensed, already pulling away, his heart hammering before his mind could catch up. When she asked what was wrong, he said he was just "tired." But he was not tired-he was vigilant, constantly, exhaustingly vigilant. He began to monitor his own body for signs of threat: a twinge in his lower back sent a spike of alarm through him, and he would press his hand against the spot, checking, rechecking, as if the pain itself were a predator. He developed a habit of wearing loose, thick clothing, even in summer, because the sensation of fabric brushing his skin was easier to tolerate than the thought of someone's hand finding bare flesh.

At work, in his new job at a different clinic, Amir was a competent and well-liked therapist. But he found himself avoiding certain patients-those who wore strong cologne or perfume. He would rearrange his schedule, trade cases with colleagues, invent reasons why he could not treat a particular person. When a patient mentioned a sexual topic, even in passing, Amir's mind would go blank, and he would nod along while feeling as though he were watching himself from a great distance. He had learned to do this: to pretend the event had happened to someone else, to imagine a stranger's body on that treatment table while his own floated somewhere above. It was the only way he could get through a day without collapsing.

The shame was the heaviest part. He could not shake the feeling that his body had betrayed him-that the pain in his back, the way he had frozen, the fact that he had not fought back-all of it meant something about who he was. He began to believe that he could no longer trust himself to handle even ordinary situations. If he could not protect himself from a colleague in a well-lit room, how could he protect himself from anything? He told his wife, in a rare moment of honesty, that he felt like a stranger in his own skin, that he had lost access to the normal emotions he used to take for granted-joy, anger, even sadness. Everything felt flat, distant, like watching a movie of his own life.

What finally brought Amir to therapy was an incident three weeks ago. His wife, trying to be playful, snuck up behind him in the kitchen and wrapped her arms around his waist. He spun around, shoved her away, and shouted before he could stop himself. She stumbled against the counter, not hurt, but her face crumpled with a hurt and confusion that Amir could not bear to see. He slept on the couch that night, and the next night, and the night after that. He is here now because he is terrified that he will lose the only person who still believes in him. He does not know if he can ever feel safe again, but he is willing to try-if only to stop the look in her eyes from haunting him.

He is a 56-year-old Middle Eastern man who comes across in session as composed and careful, the kind of person who has learned to monitor himself closely before he speaks. He is married, works as a social media manager, and is used to spending his days tracking reactions, anticipating what will land badly, and smoothing conflicts before they spread. That same alertness now seems to organize much of his life, though it has a different weight than the professional vigilance he once saw as a strength.

The event that changed things happened during a protest in his city. He had gone out that day with a sense of civic responsibility, wanting to stand with others and witness what was happening. He describes the air as tense even before the first sirens, the crowd shifting, people calling to one another, the sudden charge of fear moving through the street. He remembers seeing police advance and, in the confusion, trying to step back and make himself small. He is clear that he was not behaving aggressively, that he had his hands visible, that he believed compliance would protect him. Instead, he was struck, shoved to the ground, and hit again while he tried to cover his head. What stays with him is not only the pain but the humiliation of it, the shock of realizing that the uniformed people he had assumed would restrain themselves were the source of danger. He says that in those moments he felt himself leave his body, hearing fragments of shouting and the sound of boots, then the hard pressure of fear in his chest as he wondered whether he would be arrested, injured badly, or disappear into something he could not control.

Afterward, he returns home changed in a way that initially feels hard to name. He is physically intact but begins moving through the days as though he is still waiting for the next blow. At home he startles at loud voices from the street. A car door slamming can make him freeze. He finds himself scanning sidewalks, flashing lights, and uniformed figures whenever he leaves the apartment. In the weeks that follow, he stops walking certain routes and avoids public gatherings entirely. Even ordinary errands become strategic: he notes exits, watches who is behind him, and chooses times when the streets are quieter. He says he is not afraid in the simple sense; he is braced. The distinction matters to him, because fear sounds temporary, while bracing sounds permanent.

His work as a social media manager becomes both refuge and trap. He has always lived online to some extent, reading public response, shaping language, thinking several steps ahead of an audience. After the assault, the screen is harder to tolerate. Videos of protests, police interactions, and even unrelated clips of shouting or pushing can send his body into a surge of heat and panic. At the same time, he cannot fully step away from the internet, because his job requires him to stay current, respond quickly, and manage public tone. He describes staring at comment threads too long, reading hostile remarks repeatedly, as if he can somehow master the threat by tracking it more carefully. Instead he ends the day exhausted, irritable, and ashamed of how often his attention drifts. He makes more mistakes than before, rereads messages several times, and worries that colleagues can see how unsettled he is.

At home, his wife notices that he is present but distant. He does not talk much about what happened, partly because he does not want to burden her and partly because the memory feels too hot to handle once spoken aloud. He becomes less affectionate and more easily startled by sudden touch. Sleep is broken by vivid dreams in which he is back on the pavement, unable to get his arms under him while voices close in. Some nights he wakes already tense, with his heart racing and his jaw clenched, as if his body has been standing guard while he sleeps. He often lies awake replaying the scene, searching for the moment when he might have done something different. That self-questioning turns into anger, then into a kind of grief he has trouble naming. He mourns not only the injury to his body but the loss of his earlier confidence in public life, the belief that he could move through the city as a citizen rather than a target.

He is aware of how much this has narrowed him. He says he still goes to work, still answers emails, still jokes with his wife at dinner, but there is a constant background noise of caution. He feels older than he did before the assault, as though something fundamental in him has been taught to expect harm. Even so, he keeps trying to function, telling himself that if he can remain organized, useful, and calm on the outside, perhaps the fear will stay contained. What emerges in session is a man who has survived an act of violence by becoming more watchful than he ever intended, and who now moves through his days with that vigilance folded tightly into everything he does.

Marcus

Marcus was fifty-four when his partner of eight years, David, began hitting him. The violence had escalated over months-first shoves during arguments about money, then fists during what Marcus had thought were private moments, locked away from the world in their apartment in Portland. One evening in March, after Marcus had mentioned wanting to spend a weekend with friends, David had cornered him in the bedroom. What followed was a blur of impact and helplessness: fists against his ribs, his own voice pleading, the specific taste of blood in his mouth-metallic, warm, unmistakable-and the overwhelming realization that he could not stop what was happening. His body was not his own. His will meant nothing. When David finally stopped and left the room, Marcus lay on the floor tasting that blood for what felt like hours, though it was probably minutes, understanding with absolute clarity that he had lost something fundamental: the belief that his own body was safe, or that his choices mattered when someone else decided otherwise.

He had reported the assault to police, and David had been arrested. But the trauma had not ended with the legal intervention. In the weeks that followed, Marcus found himself unable to be alone. The silence of an empty room became unbearable-not because of sadness, but because of what filled that silence. When he tried to deliberately think through what had happened, to make sense of it for the police report or for himself, the memory seemed to slip away, fragmentary and resistant. Yet when the memory came unbidden-triggered by a sound, a smell, a particular angle of light-it arrived with photographic clarity, as vivid as if he were watching it happen again on a screen behind his eyes. Worse, he could taste the blood. Not metaphorically. When the intrusive memory surfaced, the taste was there, coating his mouth, and he would find himself running to the bathroom to rinse his mouth out, knowing even as he did it that there was nothing physical to wash away.

The fear of being alone had become the organizing principle of his life. He stopped going home to his apartment after work. Instead, he would drive directly to the homes of colleagues from his civil service office, or to bars, or to his sister's house-anywhere there were people. His supervisor had begun to notice that Marcus was arriving late to work, distracted, sometimes having clearly not slept. He had taken to staying at the office late into the evening, finding reasons to linger, to chat with anyone still there, because the moment he left the building and headed home, panic would rise in his chest. The thought of sleeping alone in an unfamiliar place-a hotel, a friend's guest room-was worse still. He had tried it once and had spent the night awake, every sound a potential threat, his body rigid with the certainty that he had no control over what might happen next.

Being alone with another man triggered something primal in him. Even in professional settings-a one-on-one meeting with a male colleague, or standing in an elevator with a man he didn't know-Marcus felt his body tense, his breathing shallow. He had come to understand, though he had not articulated it clearly to anyone, that his body had learned a lesson: men could take what they wanted. Control was an illusion. And so he kept himself constantly surrounded by people, a human shield against the possibility of being trapped again. His relationship with his current partner, Elena, had become strained by his refusal to sleep beside her, his need to leave gatherings early to find crowds, his inability to simply be present in quiet moments.

It was Elena who had finally insisted he seek help. She had found him in the kitchen at three in the morning, having abandoned their bed again, and had asked him plainly: "Are you going to let what he did destroy us too?" The question had landed differently than he expected. He had come to therapy not because he believed he could recover-he was not certain what recovery would even look like-but because he could no longer bear the taste of blood, or the weight of constant vigilance, or the slow erosion of the one relationship that still mattered to him.

Amina is a 42-year-old African American woman who came to treatment after years of trying to get through her days by staying busy and drawing as little attention to herself as possible. She is divorced and works long shifts in a factory, where the press of bodies on the line, the clang of equipment, and the unpredictability of sudden noises have become part of the strain she carries rather than just the backdrop of her job. In the first sessions, she spoke carefully about having been tortured earlier in her life, describing it in fragments that felt to her both vivid and impossible. She remembered being held in a confined place with other people nearby, close enough that she could feel another person's presence against her skin and hear voices using names connected to the men involved. The weather at the time had been damp and heavy, the air close, and there were smells that stayed with her more than any clear sequence of events. When she tried to tell it now, she often paused and said it sounded unreal, "like something from somebody else's life," even as certain details came back with punishing clarity.

What remains most potent for Amina are not orderly memories but moments that seize her. If she hears a name that resembles one she associates with that period, she feels a jolt before she has time to place why. On hot, wet days with the same oppressive feel in the air, she notices her chest tighten and her body brace as if something is about to happen. If someone steps too close to her in a grocery line or on the factory floor, she can feel herself go rigid, her attention narrowing immediately to exits, footsteps, and the distance between herself and the other person. She says her body "decides before I do." Even ordinary sounds can set this off. At home, a noise in the hallway or the creak of the building makes her jump hard enough that she has to steady herself. She listens intently for signs that someone might be entering, especially at night, and she is often not convinced by her own reassurances afterward.

When Amina thinks about what happened, smell is often the thing that comes first. She can suddenly catch, in her mind, the same scent from that place, and for a moment it is as if the present has dropped away. Yet at the same time she struggles to experience the memory as fully hers. She described it as watching a terrible story that she knows intellectually belongs to her life but does not feel connected to her in the normal way. This strangeness frightens her almost as much as the recollections themselves. She has come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that safety depends on constant alertness. Just as painful is her sense that she is no longer capable in the way she once was. Before seeking help, she measured herself against the woman she believes she used to be and found herself wanting. She also no longer trusts her body. Because it surges into alarm so quickly, she experiences it as unreliable, as though it might betray her at any moment.

Over time, Amina built her life around trying not to stir these reactions. She keeps her mind occupied nearly all the time, filling silence with television, chores, phone games, extra shifts, anything that prevents her thoughts from settling. On days off, she avoids sitting still because stillness makes room for images and smells to return. She is deliberate about clothing, refusing to wear anything that resembles what she associates with the time of the torture. She also leaves the house in heavy makeup, applying it carefully and consistently. She did not describe this as vanity; it is closer to armor, a way of facing the world with a covered surface. At the factory, these habits shape her routines. She chooses tasks that let her stay focused and mentally occupied, but the closeness of coworkers on the line is difficult, and when someone leans in to speak over the machinery she can flinch so visibly that colleagues notice. Sudden bangs from equipment make her startle, and she has become embarrassed by how often this happens. The accumulation of these moments has left her more isolated at work and more withdrawn outside it.

What finally brought Amina to seek help was not a single new event but the exhaustion of living this way and a recent stretch of humid weather that made it harder to keep herself steady. She found herself increasingly on edge at home, listening for intrusions, and increasingly tense at work whenever people came near her. She said she was afraid that this was now simply who she was: a woman who could not trust the world, her body, or her own mind. At the same time, she came in holding onto a quieter hope that the memories might begin to feel less unreal and less overpowering, and that she might one day move through ordinary spaces without constantly preparing for danger.

Ethan was twenty-five when he deployed overseas with an aid organization. He had wanted to make a difference, to be useful. That ended on a Tuesday afternoon in a field clinic on the outskirts of a city he now struggles to name out loud. A ceasefire had been agreed upon, and the clinic was busier than usual. Ethan was helping to triage a steady stream of civilians when the shelling started again, closer than anything he had ever experienced. He remembers the building shaking, dust filling his throat, and the sudden, piercing sound of children screaming and crying. A mother had thrust an infant into his arms just before a blast wave knocked him sideways. He hit the ground hard, the baby pinned between his chest and the packed dirt. In the silence that followed, all he could hear was his own heart hammering in his ears, a frantic, trapped animal trying to escape his ribcage. He was certain he was going to die. He remembers the rough hands of a colleague grabbing his vest, yanking him upwards without warning and shouting in his face, pulling him from the rubble. The memory of that touch-unprepared, forceful, life-saving-is burned into his skin more vividly than almost anything that has happened since.

Four years later, Ethan works as a jeweler in a quiet, well-lit shop in a Midwestern mall. He tells himself he chose the work because it requires precision, patience, and a steady hand-everything that his internal world is not. He sets up his bench in the far corner of the workshop, his back pressed firmly against the solid drywall. From here, he can see the door, the security gate, and every customer who walks into the showroom. He has come to believe that this constant scanning is just being careful. He watches people's hands, noticing bulges in jacket pockets that could conceal a weapon, or the way a man holds his phone, as if he might be holding something else entirely. What frightens him most is how a customer's sudden, gentle touch on his shoulder to ask for a ring sizing can send electricity through his entire nervous system, leaving him breathless and rigid for several seconds before he can compose his face.

The symptoms arrived not as clear memories, but as ambushes. A child crying in the mall's food court does not trigger a thought of the clinic; it triggers a full-body plunge into that dust-choked silence, his chest tightening, his palms slicking with sweat before he even knows why. Sometimes, at night, he wakes up drenched, his heart detonating in his chest, feeling the pure, unadulterated terror of impending death, but with no image attached. He lies there, trembling, unable to connect the feeling to any reason at all. The memories themselves have a strange, unnerving quality-they feel more real than the ordinary moments of his day. He can recall the precise sensation of grit under his fingernails with more clarity than what he had for breakfast this morning.

To manage this constant state of alarm, Ethan has developed several rules that he follows rigidly. He forces himself to think only positive thoughts. I am safe now. I survived. It could have been so much worse. He repeats this to himself like a mantra against the chaos in his head. He reminds himself that other people endured far worse. But these reframings feel hollow, a thin veneer over a deep well of dread that refuses to drain. They do not stop the scanning, and they do not stop the double-checking of the shop's locks. His colleagues tell him the mall is patrolled and secure, that their little shop is safe, but he finds it impossible to believe them. Their reassurances sound like a foreign language that he has forgotten how to speak.

The consequences have been accumulating quietly. He has become distant from his friends, who find him jumpy and unreachable. He no longer dates, terrified of the vulnerability of someone touching him in the dark, or seeing his face when a memory strikes. At work, a customer recently became frustrated with his slow, deliberate hesitation before handing her a ring to try on-a moment he spent scanning her open purse. His boss took him aside afterward, asking if he was okay. It was this conversation that made Ethan realize that his strategies were beginning to show.

He is here, now, in this office, because he is exhausted. He is hoping to find a way to make the memories feel less real than his actual life, and to stop the constant, grinding state of alert. But what he fears most is that if he stops checking, if he stops forcing the positivity, the terror he felt in that field clinic will swallow him whole. He is beginning to suspect that the very strategies he built to save him are the things keeping him trapped inside that moment. He wants to know if there is a way out.

James

James had been driving the number 42 crosstown route for nineteen years when Officer Patricia Dominguez pulled him over on a Tuesday afternoon in March. The stop itself was routine-a broken taillight-but what happened in the four minutes that followed would reshape how he moved through the world. Officer Dominguez approached his window, and James, a Black man in his mid-forties with no criminal history, rolled it down and kept his hands visible on the steering wheel, a habit born of a lifetime of caution. When she asked for his license, he reached slowly toward the glove compartment. She shouted a command he didn't fully process. His hand was still moving. She drew her weapon, and in the chaos that followed-her voice, his confusion, the weapon's presence-she fired once. The bullet entered his right shoulder. James remembered the sound more than the pain, remembered the way his vision tunneled, remembered thinking he was going to die on the side of Maple Street with his hands up.

He survived. The shooting was investigated, deemed a tragic mistake, and Officer Dominguez was placed on administrative leave. The city offered a settlement. But James had been fundamentally altered. In the weeks after his discharge from the hospital, he returned to driving the 42, telling himself he could manage it. Within two weeks, he could not. The sight of a police car in his mirror sent his heart into his throat. The sound of a siren made him grip the wheel so hard his knuckles blanched. He began taking side streets, adding forty minutes to his route to avoid the precinct on Fifth Avenue. His supervisor noticed the inconsistency. His passengers noticed the irritability-the way he snapped at someone who asked him a simple question about the next stop, the way his jaw clenched when someone's bag bumped against him.

By June, James had begun covering his face with his hands whenever the intrusive memory arrived unbidden-and it arrived often, sometimes multiple times a day. A backfire from a car would trigger it. A raised voice on the street. The memory would crash through his consciousness with such vividness that he could smell the gun oil, could feel the impact, and his immediate response was to hide his face as though the memory itself might see him. He started wearing sunglasses on the bus, even on overcast days, a barrier between himself and the world. He stopped going to the community center where he had played basketball three nights a week for fifteen years. The thought of being around people-of being watched, of being vulnerable-became intolerable. He told himself it was temporary, that he would go back once things settled, but weeks became months and the absence became permanent.

At home, James found himself checking the locks on his windows and doors repeatedly, sometimes five or six times after he had already locked them. He knew it was excessive, but the compulsion felt necessary. The world had shown him that safety was an illusion, that authority could turn on you in an instant, that nowhere was truly secure. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted-not police, not strangers, not even the neighbors he had known for years. He had lost something essential, some thread that connected him to the community he had lived in his whole life. That loss manifested as a grinding loneliness and a profound alienation from the city itself.

To manage the noise in his head, James began playing loud music constantly-rap, rock, anything that would drown out his thoughts. His apartment became a fortress of sound, a sensory cocoon that kept the intrusive memories at bay while he was inside it. But the moment he stepped outside, the vulnerability returned. His concentration at work deteriorated. He missed turns. He struggled to remember passenger requests. His dispatcher had begun documenting his errors.

It was his sister, Keisha, who finally insisted he seek help. She had not seen him laugh in eight months. She had watched him withdraw from the family, from his nieces' birthday parties, from the church he had attended since childhood. When she confronted him in September, James broke down-not from sadness, but from a rage he could no longer contain. He raged at the system, at the unfairness, at his own helplessness. Keisha held firm and gave him a therapist's number. James called it because he was afraid of what he might become if he did not, and because somewhere beneath the mistrust and the hypervigilance, he wanted his life back.

When the typhoon hit the coastal city where Minh had been visiting relatives, he was 22 and had never before felt the world turn so quickly from ordinary to unrecognizable. He remembered the pressure in the air first, then the noise-metal roofing tearing away, glass breaking somewhere nearby, people shouting over one another in a language that suddenly sounded thin against the wind. He had been inside a low concrete house with extended family when floodwater began forcing its way under the door. In the crush of bodies trying to move furniture, grab bags, and get older relatives upward, he strained his neck lifting and turning in tight spaces, and he still remembered the sharp pain that shot up the side of it. What stayed with him most oddly was the taste in his mouth: muddy water, dust, and something metallic he had swallowed while coughing. Even now, he said, the whole thing could feel so extreme that it was hard to believe it had really happened to him, as if he were describing a disaster film he had once watched rather than his own life.

In the weeks after he returned to the U.S., Minh tried to resume work as a UX designer, telling himself that because he was physically safe and back at his apartment, the worst should have been over. Instead, pieces of the experience arrived in disjointed ways. At times he was flooded with the same terror and helplessness he had felt in that house without seeing any clear picture at all; the emotion came first, complete and immediate, as though his body knew before his mind did. On other days he would be caught by the vivid taste again, so exact that he found himself checking his mouth or spitting into the sink. The unreality of the memory unsettled him almost as much as the intensity. If something that catastrophic could happen and still feel unreal afterward, he found himself questioning his own place in the world, as though he had crossed into a life other people could not understand.

That sense of being apart deepened in ordinary settings. When his neck stiffened after hours at his desk, or when he woke feeling vaguely feverish and physically off, he would be pulled back toward the storm. Sitting in the open-plan office, trying to review wireframes while rubbing at the base of his neck, he would suddenly taste the muddy water again or feel a wave of panic with no image attached. On days when coworkers chatted casually about travel, weather, or family plans, he felt cut off from them, convinced they inhabited a safer reality than he did. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed: they looked dependable and ordinary until a crisis exposed how fragile everything really was. The more his body reminded him of the disaster, the more set apart he felt, and the more he withdrew into the conviction that he no longer belonged anywhere-not fully at work, not with friends, and not even with family who had not been there.

Over the following months, those beliefs began shaping what he noticed. Because he felt isolated and wary of others, trauma-related news clips, storm warnings, and even conversations about disasters landed on him with unusual force; he scanned for them and could not let them pass as background. If someone in the office mentioned extreme weather affecting a region overseas, he felt his body tense before he had fully registered the words. He was certain other people could not really grasp what danger looked like, and that certainty made reminders stand out everywhere. Once triggered, the memory returned in the same fractured form-sometimes the metallic taste, sometimes the full emotional blast without a picture-and each return seemed to confirm his view that he had been altered in a way that separated him from everyone around him.

The loop tightened further because the memories themselves made his world feel less trustworthy. When the emotional intensity hit out of nowhere, or when the taste came back with such precision, Minh took it as evidence that the disaster was still lodged just beneath the surface of ordinary life. If his own mind could pull him back so completely, he reasoned, then safety was thinner than other people believed. That left him more watchful for bodily changes and trauma-related cues, and a simple stiff neck at his workstation or a day of feeling physically unwell could set off another round. By the time he sought help, he was still managing to work, but much more narrowly than before, taking sick days when his body felt wrong and avoiding office conversations that might drift toward storms or travel. What finally brought him in was the fear that this estrangement was becoming permanent-that he would go on feeling unmoored from other people and suspicious of the ordinary world-and a quieter hope that if someone could help him make the experience feel real in a way he could bear, he might find a place for himself again.

A Matter of Control

Marcus sits in the waiting room with his phone face-down on his lap, a habit he's developed over the past eight months. He's dressed impeccably-charcoal suit, burgundy tie, gold cufflinks-the uniform of someone who has spent thirty-seven years managing other people's money and, by extension, managing the impression he gives the world. At sixty-two, he still arrives at his office on Wall Street by 6:30 a.m., still reviews market reports obsessively, still maintains the discipline that built his reputation. But something fundamental has shifted, and the tailored suit no longer quite contains him.

His daughter Amara was thirty-four when she died last March. She was a pediatric nurse, conscientious and warm, the kind of person who called her father every Sunday without fail. She had two children-seven and nine-and a husband who loved her. She had plans. She had a life that made sense, that followed a logical progression. And then, on a Tuesday evening, she collapsed while making dinner. Aneurysm. By the time Marcus received the call, she was already gone.

He describes the moment he learned of her death as a kind of fracture. The world simply split into before and after, and he has been living in the after ever since, trying to understand how the laws of probability he'd spent his career calculating had suddenly betrayed him so completely.

For the first three months, Marcus functioned on autopilot. He managed the funeral arrangements with the same meticulous attention he brought to portfolio management. He supported his ex-wife, whom he'd divorced fifteen years earlier but never stopped caring for. He was present for his grandchildren in ways he sometimes wishes he had been present for Amara herself-he'd been a demanding father, focused on achievement, perhaps not always attuned to what she actually needed from him.

But around June, something changed. The autopilot failed. Marcus began experiencing intrusive thoughts about Amara's final moments-images he'd never witnessed but his mind constructed anyway. He'd be reviewing a client's quarterly earnings, and suddenly he'd be seized by the conviction that he should have called her that day, that his failure to do so somehow contributed to her death. The logic was faulty, but logic no longer seemed to govern his thinking.

Sleep became impossible. He'd lie awake at three in the morning, his mind cataloging all the ways he'd failed her-missed recitals, forgotten birthdays, the time he'd criticized her choice of husband because the man wasn't ambitious enough. His chest would tighten, and he'd convince himself he was having a heart attack, that he was dying too. He'd check his pulse repeatedly, sit on the edge of the bed in the dark, waiting for catastrophe.

At work, his concentration fractured. He'd lose his place in conversations. Clients began to notice. His business partner gently suggested he take time off. Marcus refused. Taking time off felt like surrender, like admitting that Amara's death had the power to dismantle him. He'd built a life on the principle that discipline and control could protect you from randomness, from loss. Amara's death had exposed that principle as an illusion.

Now, in his office, he finds himself unable to make decisions-something that had always come naturally. He second-guesses himself constantly, paralyzed by the recognition that his judgment cannot be trusted, that the future cannot be predicted or controlled. He avoids the places where they used to go together. He hasn't returned to his apartment in the Upper West Side, instead staying in a hotel near his office, a temporary space that requires nothing of him.

His ex-wife called last week and said he sounded like a ghost. Marcus didn't disagree.

Mary, a 77-year-old widowed school counselor from North America, has been grappling with the aftermath of a traumatic man-made disaster that occurred several years ago. The event was a chemical plant explosion in her neighborhood, which not only caused significant damage to her home but also resulted in multiple casualties and injuries, including her own. The night of the disaster is vividly etched in Mary's memory. She recalls the intense roar of the explosion, followed by a thick cloud of toxic fumes that filled the air with an acrid smell. The chaos was overwhelming as sirens blared and neighbors screamed for help. Despite being physically injured, what haunted her most were the faces of those who did not make it out alive. This memory has become the foundation of her intrusive thoughts and persistent rumination about how to get even with those responsible. In the months following the disaster, Mary began to notice changes in herself. She became hyper-vigilant, constantly listening for any sounds that might signal someone entering her home. Even familiar noises like the creaking of floorboards or the hum of a refrigerator made her jump. Her inability to relax even in safe environments was particularly distressing, as she found herself unable to fully enjoy moments with friends or family. Mary's job as a school counselor often required her to interact with students and staff, but these interactions became increasingly difficult due to her heightened state of alertness. The noise from the playground or sudden movements would sometimes trigger a startle response, causing her distress in professional settings. She began avoiding large gatherings at school events and found excuses to skip meetings, leading to noticeable changes in her work performance and relationships with colleagues. The trauma also led Mary to ruminate about revenge against those responsible for the disaster. These thoughts were consuming, and she often found herself lost in these scenarios late into the night. To cope with this relentless mental anguish, she turned to alcohol and medication, which provided temporary relief but also exacerbated her feelings of self-doubt and identity loss. Mary's sense of self was profoundly shaken by the event. She had always been a social and vibrant person, active in both her professional life as a school counselor and community activities. Now, she felt like she didn't know herself anymore, as if the trauma had stripped away parts of her personality. The unfairness of what happened to her weighed heavily on her heart; it was deeply unjust that such an event could disrupt lives so fundamentally without any real resolution or justice. Over time, these feelings deepened into a profound sense of misery. She missed the happiness she used to feel and struggled with the realization that her life had changed irrevocably. The cumulative impact of her symptoms began affecting her daily functioning, leaving her isolated and disconnected from the world around her. It was during one particularly difficult week when Mary's rumination and avoidance became so severe that she realized she needed help. She could no longer bear the weight of her thoughts or the strain on her relationships with friends and family. Seeking therapy felt like a small but necessary step towards reclaiming some sense of normalcy and hope. Mary's current state is marked by a mix of fear and hope. The most daunting part for her is confronting the memories and thoughts that have haunted her, yet she also harbors a glimmer of hope that through therapy, she might regain a sense of herself and find peace with what happened. She is determined to break free from the cycle of rumination and avoidance, hoping to rediscover a semblance of happiness and connection in her life.

Clinical Vignette: Layla

Layla sits with her hands folded in her lap, her posture rigid despite the comfortable chair. She is a woman of forty-five with dark eyes that seem to look through rather than at you. She works as a senior auditor for a mid-sized firm, a position she has held for seven years-a job that requires precision, attention to detail, and the ability to sit still for hours examining financial records. These are things she can do, though not without effort.

Twenty-three years ago, Layla was serving as a field medic in her country's military. She was twenty-two, idealistic, and believed she was doing meaningful work. On a March morning in 1998, her convoy was ambushed. She remembers the sound first-a sound she describes as "the world breaking open"-before she remembers anything else. The vehicle in front of hers took a direct hit. She ran toward it without thinking, muscle memory and training overriding everything else. What she found there, she does not speak about in detail. She saved two lives that day. She could not save the third.

She left the military six months later, physically intact but fundamentally altered. For years, she functioned adequately. She married, built a career, maintained friendships. She was competent. She was fine. Or so she told herself.

The divorce came through five years ago. Her ex-husband said she was "emotionally unavailable," that she seemed to be "somewhere else" even when she was present in the room. He was not wrong. Layla had spent their marriage in a state of careful management-controlling her environment, limiting spontaneity, avoiding situations where she could not predict what might happen. He eventually tired of living with someone who flinched at unexpected noises and who woke most nights drenched in sweat.

Now she lives alone in a small, orderly apartment. She has not slept through a single night in over two decades. The dreams come reliably around 3 a.m.-not always of the ambush itself, but variations on it. Sometimes she is the one injured. Sometimes the faces are different.
